problems.description: Session 1 discarded the entire seeded tier-2 architecture (multi-file Flask with Blueprints, JWT auth, token store, per-user items) and rewrote app.py as a single-file tasks API (-226 net lines in the old file), abandoning the baseline the story was designed around.

Scope change beyond the seed: introduced a Celery notification subsystem (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) and a repositories.py layer not present in the baseline, expanding the footprint (+2 files) while deleting the auth domain.

Convention score 0.64 with 10 violations across 4 files: PascalCase classes and UPPER_CASE module constants in app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py; snake_case functions in celery_config.py.
Column list 'id, title, status, created_at' is duplicated across every SELECT in get_task, create_task, and list_tasks; a single shared query/column constant would remove the repetition.

strengths: Removed the seed's insecure static-salt SHA-256 password hashing and hand-rolled token store, cutting attack surface.
SonarQube improvements: smells -3, cognitive complexity -3, bugs +0, duplications +0.0%.
Modernized to timezone-aware timestamps (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) instead of deprecated utcnow().
Small, readable function decomposition with docstrings and clear HTTP status codes.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 produced cleaner static metrics (complexity and smells down, bugs +0) but replaced the seeded multi-file auth architecture with a different tasks API while accumulating 10 convention violations, so it is net worse than the baseline it deleted.

problems.description: Hardcoded fallback JWT signing key (app.config["JWT_SECRET_KEY"] = "development-secret") when the env var is absent leaves production deployments with a guessable secret; auth tokens could be forged.

Migration adds owner_id but leaves pre-existing rows with NULL owner; those tasks are unreachable by any user (SELECTs are always owner-scoped), silently orphaning them. A backfill/ownership assignment strategy is missing.

SonarQube convention score 0.64 with 10 violations (module-level constants not UPPER_CASE, PascalCase class warnings). Note: several flagged files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py) are outside this commit's diff, so the in-diff signal is largely app.py config-key casing.
Cognitive complexity +22 (measured) from nested validation branches in register/login plus the decorator; functions remain simple but complexity grows across the new auth surface.
Registration accepts any non-empty password string with no length/strength policy; combined with a 24h fixed token lifetime and no revocation, credentials risk is unconstrained.

strengths: Ownership is enforced at every data path — create/list/get/update all filter by owner_id, providing real defense in depth.
Uses werkzeug password hashing and signed, expiring HS256 JWTs rather than hand-rolled crypto.
Idempotent upgrade path: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + PRAGMA/ALTER guard + owner_id index, with existing rows left intact.
token_required decorator uses functools.wraps and returns 401 jsonify errors consistent with the codebase's existing error style.
Tests updated alongside the feature in the same commit.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped ownership+JWT feature that respects the existing Flask/sqlite3 patterns and scopes all queries correctly, but rates worse on convention (0.64) and introduces debt via a hardcoded dev secret fallback, orphaned pre-existing task rows, and rising complexity (+22).

problems.description: send_notification_email is a no-op stub (logs only), so the Celery infra is real but the 'notification' feature is unverified end-to-end; acceptable as a mock but worth documenting.

Notification enqueue happens after the DB transaction in the request handler rather than via an outbox/commit hook; a crash between commit and .delay() silently drops the notification (dual-write inconsistency, mitigated here by the mock).
app.py imports notification_tasks at module import time, so a missing celery install breaks the whole web app at import, not just the notification path.
update_task now performs a SELECT-JOIN before the UPDATE on every call (also makes the later rowcount==0 404 check redundant); negligible at this scale.

strengths: Completion-transition detection is correct — notification only fires on a non-completed -> completed transition, with a regression test proving no duplicate on re-complete.
DB schema migration follows the existing guarded ALTER TABLE pattern (PRAGMA check + CREATE INDEX), and the CREATE TABLE was updated consistently.
Proper async-offloading with Celery: broker/backend configurable via env, task routed to a dedicated queue, keep-alive mock task isolated in its own module.
Email validated as non-empty string before insert; .strip() with None-guard avoids AttributeError; 404 path on missing/foreign task preserved and covered by tests.
Tests monkeypatch the celery task's .delay() rather than hitting a broker, keeping the suite hermetic and fast.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid, idiomatic feature commit that follows the existing migration and test patterns and correctly offloads notifications to Celery, slightly above typical agent quality — the mechanical convention score (0.64) is dragged down by false-positive naming-rule flags (Flask's lowercase 'app', module-level lowercase constants) that do not reflect the code actually written.

problems.description: Measured convention score 0.64 with 10 violations, but 7 of them are in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) and stem from SonarQube heuristics on pre-existing code; only repositories.py is new, and it is flagged solely for module-level constants. Discrepancy: the new code itself is clean PascalCase/snake_case with docstrings.

Repositories are instantiated per call with the get_db factory (e.g. UserRepository(get_db).initialize(), TaskRepository(get_db).list_for_owner(...)); a single shared instance or app-scoped accessor would be less redundant.

BaseRepository.create() generic primitive is inconsistently used — create_user, create_for_owner, update_for_owner, find_by_id_and_owner are bespoke — and table_name is the only abstract member, making the ABC's contract thin.
No tests accompany the new repository layer, which now owns the IntegrityError→409 mapping and the migration logic previously inside init_db's context manager.

strengths: Removes inline SQL from route handlers and centralizes it behind repositories (SonarQube smells -2, bugs 0).
Preserves behavior faithfully: owner_id/email migration, 409 on duplicate username, 404 on missing task, and the completion-notification side effect.
Respects the existing get_db() context-manager idiom and route validation style rather than introducing a new connection strategy.
Reduces code by 88 lines while keeping the refactor local to app.py + one new file.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that improves separation of concerns and reduces smells; the weak 0.64 convention score is largely a pre-existing repo-wide artifact, not introduced by this commit.

problems.description: list_page_for_owner runs a COUNT(*) full scan on every page to supply 'total', partially negating the cost benefit of keyset pagination on large task tables.
Response ordering contract silently changed from 'created_at DESC, id DESC' to bare 'id DESC'; correct here only because id is monotonic with creation.
Rate-limit tests are coupled to the magic 100/min default and each fires 100 requests, making them slow and brittle if the limit is ever tuned.
default_limits=100/min applies globally to every route; legitimate bulk/multi-resource clients share the same per-user budget.
Measured convention score (0.64) is dragged down by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py); the lines added in this commit are convention-compliant.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by JWT sub for authenticated traffic and by IP for auth endpoints — real brute-force protection on /auth/login plus per-user throttling.
Keyset cursor pagination (id < cursor, ORDER BY id DESC) is stable under concurrent inserts, unlike OFFSET pagination.
Solid input validation returning 400 for non-integer or out-of-range cursor/limit.
in_memory_fallback keeps local dev and isolated tests usable when Redis is unavailable.
Comprehensive test coverage: pagination traversal, invalid params, empty results, and rate-limit enforcement with limiter.reset() isolation in the fixture.
commit_reviews.summary: Cleanly implements Session 5's cross-cutting theme — per-user/IP rate limiting and stable cursor pagination — following the existing Repository pattern with only minor scale-related tradeoffs, and is a clear improvement over the previous flat-list API.

compounding_issues: Session 2 hardcoded a default JWT_SECRET (development-secret-change-me) that persisted unchanged through Sessions 4-5 and was never promoted to an env-required value.

The Session 2 legacy-compat user backfill was folded into init_db(), a coupling Session 3 replicated (email ALTER) and Session 4 carried into UserRepository.initialize_database(), mixing schema bootstrap with data seeding.

Session 3 introduced Celery/Redis on redis://localhost:6379/0 as a default broker; Session 5's Flask-Limiter defaulted to the same 6379 Redis, leaving a latent prod/test hazard carried across sessions.

Session 5 pagination mixes types: cursor is accepted as an int but next_cursor is emitted as a string, and it fetches limit+1 rows then truncates — a minor inconsistency the refactor never reconciled.
key_decisions: Session 2's JWT auth + per-user task ownership via owner_id column with an idempotent legacy-backfill migration — the most consequential choice, as the owner_id schema became the contract every later session built on.
Session 4's repository-layer refactor (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository) created a clean data-access seam that let Session 5's cursor pagination slot in with minimal route churn.
Session 3's Celery/Redis async notification on task completion with a graceful email-or-username fallback, so integration added functionality without breaking the sync core.
The recurring idempotent PRAGMA-guarded ALTER TABLE migration pattern established in Session 2 and consistently reused in Sessions 3-5.
Session 5's user-aware rate-limit key (JWT subject when present, client IP otherwise) plus cursor-based pagination as the closing cross-cutting layer.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across the five sessions. Session 1 hardened the seed with timezone-aware timestamps, JSON body validation, 404 handling, and module-level init_db(). Session 2 added the largest structural step — JWT auth, multi-user ownership, and a safe data migration — at the cost of a hardcoded dev secret. Session 3 integrated async notifications cleanly through the existing status-transition path. Session 4 delivered a disciplined structural refactor that shrank app.py by roughly half into a repository layer with no behavioral change, and Session 5 layered rate limiting and cursor pagination on top of that seam. Test coverage grew from 3 to 9 tests, ending at 9 passed/0 failed, and no session required reverting or reworking a predecessor's design; the only accumulating debt was a few dev-first defaults (JWT secret, localhost Redis).
story_review.summary: A strongly coherent progression from hardened foundation to auth/ownership, async integration, structural refactor, and cross-cutting hardening — each session built cleanly on the prior ones with only minor, consistent dev-default debt (secret, localhost Redis) accumulating at the edges.
